title: Unit 6 test: Integration and Accumulation of Change
author: bc-tests-extensions
directions: Original Liminal practice. Section I Part A and Section II Part B are without a calculator; the other parts require a graphing calculator. Show supporting work and justify conclusions in free response. Angles are in radians. Use exact answers without a calculator and three decimal places for calculator work unless a question specifies otherwise. Report raw practice points only.

figures.alt: Line segments connect (0, 2), (1, 4), (3, −2), and (4, 0) on a graph of signed flow q against time t.

parts.title: No calculator
parts.directions: Select one answer for each question.

items.prompt: A tank contains 7 L at t = 0. Its signed net flow q is the piecewise linear function shown. How much liquid is in the tank at t = 4 minutes?
items.rationale: The signed trapezoid areas are 3, 2, and −1 L. Thus the net addition is 4 L, and the final amount is 7 + 4 = 11 L.

distractorNotes.A: This is the net change, not the final amount.
distractorNotes.B: This replaces the last negative triangular contribution by a positive contribution.
distractorNotes.D: This subtracts the signed integral instead of adding it.

items.prompt: Which definite integral is represented by lim as n → ∞ of Σ from i = 1 to n of (3/n)(2 + 3i/n)^2?
items.rationale: The width is Δx = 3/n and the right endpoints are 2 + iΔx, so the interval is [2, 5].

distractorNotes.B: The sample points start at 2, not 0.
distractorNotes.C: The interval has width 3, not right endpoint 3.
distractorNotes.D: The factor 3 is already included in the interval width.

items.prompt: Let F(x) = ∫ from 1 to x^2 of ln(1 + t^2) dt. What is F′(x)?
items.rationale: The Fundamental Theorem and chain rule give F′(x) = ln(1 + (x^2)^2)·2x.

distractorNotes.A: This omits the derivative of the upper limit.
distractorNotes.B: The integrand must be evaluated at t = x^2.
distractorNotes.C: This differentiates the substituted integrand instead of the integral.

items.prompt: A continuous function f satisfies ∫ from −1 to 2 of f(x) dx = 6 and ∫ from 2 to 5 of f(x) dx = −3. What is ∫ from 5 to −1 of [2f(x) − 1] dx?
items.rationale: On [−1, 5], the integral is 2(6 − 3) − 6 = 0. Reversing limits still gives 0.

distractorNotes.A: This reverses the f integral but omits the constant term.
distractorNotes.C: This gives the constant contribution the wrong orientation.
distractorNotes.D: This changes the second signed integral to positive and also keeps the forward integration limits.

items.prompt: For x > −1, which is an antiderivative of (x^2 + 2x + 3)/(x + 1)?
items.rationale: Polynomial division gives x + 1 + 2/(x + 1); integrate each term. Differentiating the result recovers the integrand.

distractorNotes.B: This divides individual numerator terms without preserving the denominator.
distractorNotes.C: This integrates the remainder as an inverse square instead of an inverse first power.

items.prompt: What is ∫ from 0 to π/4 of x cos(2x) dx?
items.rationale: With u = x and dv = cos(2x) dx, an antiderivative is x sin(2x)/2 + cos(2x)/4. Evaluating from 0 to π/4 gives π/8 − 1/4 = (π − 2)/8.

distractorNotes.A: This gives the lower-endpoint cosine contribution the wrong sign.
distractorNotes.B: This retains the boundary product but omits the remaining integral.
distractorNotes.D: This loses a factor of 1/2 from integrating the trigonometric function.

items.prompt: On an interval not containing −3 or −1, which expression is an antiderivative of 1/[(x + 1)(x + 3)]?
items.rationale: The decomposition is (1/2)/(x + 1) − (1/2)/(x + 3). Its integral is the stated logarithmic difference.

distractorNotes.A: This omits the factor 1/2 in the partial fractions.
distractorNotes.C: This reverses the signs of both partial-fraction coefficients.
distractorNotes.D: This adds the fractions where their difference is required.

items.prompt: Let I = ∫ from 0 to 1 of x^(−2/3) dx and J = ∫ from 1 to ∞ of x^(−2/3) dx. Which statement is correct?
items.rationale: The antiderivative is 3x^(1/3). Its limit at zero is 0, but its limit at infinity is infinite.

distractorNotes.A: The power thresholds near zero and near infinity are different.
distractorNotes.B: The antiderivative grows without bound at infinity.
distractorNotes.C: An unbounded integrand near zero need not have a divergent integral.

parts.title: Graphing calculator
parts.directions: Select one answer. Numerical choices are rounded as displayed.

items.prompt: A calibration pulse has intensity e^(−x^2) for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. What is its integrated intensity ∫ from 0 to 2 of e^(−x^2) dx, to three decimal places?
items.rationale: Numerical integration gives 0.8820813908, so the integrated intensity is 0.882.

distractorNotes.A: This treats e^(−x^2) as though its antiderivative were −e^(−x^2)/2.
distractorNotes.C: This doubles the integral over the stated interval.
distractorNotes.D: This reports the average intensity instead of the integral.

items.prompt: A feeder adds material at rate 2 + sin(t^2) grams per minute. Starting with an empty container, at what time b > 0 does it first contain 5 grams?
items.rationale: Solve ∫ from 0 to b of [2 + sin(t^2)] dt = 5 numerically. The solution is b = 2.1808472203; the rate is at least 1, so the solution is unique.

distractorNotes.B: This assumes the rate stays at its maximum value 3.
distractorNotes.C: This does not satisfy the accumulated-mass equation.

items.prompt:
A positive rate r is sampled below. Using all three table subintervals, what is the trapezoidal estimate of ∫ from 0 to 2.7 of r(t) dt?

t | 0 | 0.6 | 1.5 | 2.7
r(t) | 4.0 | 5.2 | 4.7 | 3.1

distractorNotes.B: This uses width 0.9 for all three trapezoids.
distractorNotes.C: This is the left-endpoint sum with the actual widths.
distractorNotes.D: This is the right-endpoint sum with the actual widths.

items.prompt: The tail cost of a process is modeled by ∫ from 2 to ∞ of (ln x)/x^2 dx. Which value is correct, to three decimal places?
items.rationale: An antiderivative is −(ln x + 1)/x, whose limit at infinity is 0. The integral is (ln 2 + 1)/2 = 0.8465735903.

distractorNotes.A: This omits the integral left after integration by parts.
distractorNotes.B: This fails to divide the lower-endpoint contribution by 2.
distractorNotes.D: Although ln x grows, division by x^2 makes this integral converge.

parts.title: Graphing calculator
parts.directions: Show integral or equation setups and justify conclusions.

items.prompt: A collection system holds A(t) liters at time t minutes, where A(0) = 8 and A′(t) = q(t) = 3 + sin(t^2/2) − 0.2t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4. Define B(t) = ∫ from 0 to t^2 of q(s) ds for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2.

parts.label: a
steps: A(4) = 8 + ∫ from 0 to 4 of q(t) dt.
The integral is 11.307513420 L; add the initial amount.

rubric.criterion: Relates the final amount to the initial amount plus the integral of q.
Correctly evaluates the definite integral numerically.
Reports 19.308 L, including the initial amount and units.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find B′(1.3). Show the derivative expression before evaluating.

rubric.criterion: Evaluates q at the upper limit t^2.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the time when A(t) first reaches 15 L. Explain why there is exactly one such time on [0, 4].
parts.answer: t = 2.117 min; A is strictly increasing.
steps: Solve ∫ from 0 to t of q(s) ds = 7 to obtain 2.116984635.
Since q(t) ≥ 3 − 1 − 0.8 = 1.2 > 0 on [0, 4], A is strictly increasing.
Continuity and 8 < 15 < A(4) give existence; strict increase gives uniqueness.

rubric.criterion: Sets the accumulated addition equal to 7 and obtains t = 2.117.
Establishes q > 0 on the entire interval.
Uses continuity, endpoint amounts, and strict increase to justify existence and uniqueness.

items.prompt: Evaluate the first two integrals exactly and determine whether the third converges. Show the transformations and limiting expressions that justify each result.

parts.label: a
steps: Set u = 1 + x^2 and du = 2x dx, changing the limits to 1 and 2.
The integral is 3∫ from 1 to 2 of 1/u du = 3 ln 2.

rubric.criterion: Makes a correct substitution with differential.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: ∫ from 0 to 1 of x ln(1 + x) dx
steps: Use u = ln(1 + x), dv = x dx to obtain ln 2/2 − (1/2)∫ from 0 to 1 of x^2/(1 + x) dx.
The remaining integral is ln 2 − 1/2, so the result is 1/4.

rubric.criterion: Divides x^2 by x + 1 and integrates the result.
Combines the boundary term and remaining integral to obtain 1/4.

parts.label: c
steps: The singularity at 0 requires two one-sided integrals, each of which must converge.
For example, lim as b → 0+ of ∫ from b to 1 of x^(−2) dx = lim as b → 0+ of (1/b − 1) = ∞.
Thus the improper integral diverges; endpoint substitution across 0 is invalid.

rubric.criterion: Splits at the singularity and states that both sides must converge.
Displays a correct one-sided limit and antiderivative.
Concludes divergence from an infinite one-sided limit.
